subject: Probability and Statistics (GATE DA)
weightagePercent: 16-20% of total 100 marks (≈16-19 marks confirmed 2024-25; historically one of the top 1-2 highest-weighted of the 7 DA subjects, alongside Programming/DSA)
difficulty: Moderate-to-Hard — consistently flagged across all 3 editions (independently by GeeksforGeeks, PW Live, Careers360, Shiksha, KollegeApply, IMS) as one of the two most calculation-intensive, conceptually toughest sections of the DA paper (the other being Machine Learning), even though it is also one of the highest-scoring/highest-ROI sections if practiced well. Descriptive-stats and basic-probability items are easy 1-markers; hypothesis-testing, multi-step Bayes/tree problems, and distribution-parameter NATs are the hard tail.
pyqTrendByYear: 2024 (IISc Bengaluru): ~10 questions / 16 marks (GeeksforGeeks' question-by-question tally: 4×1-mark MCQ + 1×2-mark MCQ + 5×2-mark NAT = 16M), one of the largest sections that year but behind Programming/DSA (13Q/21M). Two dominant recurring PYQ patterns already visible: (a) a Bayes'-theorem "given priors/conditionals, find posterior" word problem, and (b) a "identify-the-distribution-then-compute mean/variance/probability" word problem. Q59 (2024, 2-mark NAT, believed statistics-adjacent) was voided (MTA - Marks To All) by IISc, evidence the toughest NAT items in this section can be genuinely flawed/ambiguous, not just hard. 2025 (IIT Roorkee): ~12 questions / 18-19 marks — corroborated by two independent counts: GeeksforGeeks' own tally (12Q/18M: 6×1-mark + 6×2-mark) and this researcher's own primary-source classification of the official answer key (12Q/19M) — the small 1-mark gap is a single boundary-classification call, not a real disagreement. This makes P&S the single highest-weighted or joint-highest-weighted of the 7 subjects in 2025 (ahead of Programming-DSA and ML, both 9Q/14M in the primary-source tally). Paper-wide in 2025, MSQ count rose and NAT count fell versus 2024, a shift toward "conceptual/properties" questions (e.g., MSQ on properties of a distribution) over pure heavy calculation — this shift plausibly touched P&S items too. 2026 (IIT Guwahati): no official or coaching numeric question-count table for this subject could be located despite targeted searches (GeeksforGeeks, PW Live's dedicated 2026 analysis page, MadeEasy) — this is a genuine reporting gap, not an oversight. However, every qualitative post-exam review available (PW Live, Shiksha, KollegeApply, Careers360) independently describes the 2026 paper as "mathematics-heavy" and "moderate-to-tough," explicitly naming Probability & Statistics (distributions, hypothesis testing, Bayesian methods) alongside ML as the most calculation-intensive/toughest areas — consistent with, not contradicting, a continued 16-19+ mark weightage. Net 3-year read (n=3, flagged as indicative not statistically robust): weightage has been stable-to-rising (16M -> 18-19M -> qualitatively "still heavy/toughest") and the question style has drifted slightly from raw NAT computation toward more MSQ-style conceptual/properties testing.
expected2027: Medium-High confidence that P&S remains a top-2 highest-weighted subject at roughly 16-20 marks (16-20%) in GATE DA 2027, and High confidence the topic list itself is unchanged — reasoning: (1) the official syllabus wording for this section has been byte-for-byte identical across all 3 editions under 3 different organizing institutes (IISc, IIT Roorkee, IIT Guwahati), so structural continuity is well-evidenced even though GATE 2027's organizing institute (likely IIT Madras per the 8-year rotation, but not yet officially confirmed as of 17 Jul 2026) hasn't published a syllabus yet; (2) weightage has held in the 16-19 mark band for both years it could be precisely measured (2024, 2025) and 2026 commentary is consistent with continuation, not decline; (3) Bayes'-theorem word problems and distribution-identification problems have recurred as signature question archetypes in every edition so far, and the paper-wide 2024->2025 drift toward more MSQ/conceptual and fewer pure-NAT questions is a plausible continuing style trend. Confidence is capped at Medium-High rather than High because: exact per-subject question counts are always coaching-derived estimates (GATE never publishes an official topic-weightage table), the sample is only n=3 editions, and 2027's organizing institute/paper-setters are unconfirmed, so a discretionary reweighting (e.g., a harder/easier P&S section, or more emphasis shifted to hypothesis testing vs Bayes) cannot be ruled out.
priorityForTopRank: High. For a time-constrained working professional targeting AIR 50-200: this is consistently one of the two highest-mark-value subjects in the entire paper (tied with/ahead of Programming-DSA), so marginal study hours here have the best expected-marks return of any subject. It is also the most cross-cutting subject in the syllabus — Bayes' theorem underpins Naive Bayes, covariance/Gaussian assumptions underpin LDA and PCA-adjacent reasoning, and CLT/estimation intuition underpins bias-variance and confidence-interval-style ML questions — so mastery here has positive spillover into the Machine Learning section (itself high-weightage) rather than being an isolated cost center. Recommended allocation: front-load descriptive stats, counting, and basic probability (cheap, high-accuracy marks) early; spend the largest single block of P&S study time on Bayes'-theorem multi-step problems, distribution identification (Binomial/Poisson/Exponential/Normal triage), and hypothesis testing (z/t/chi-squared) since these are simultaneously the highest-frequency AND highest-difficulty items — the section's difficulty is "solvable with practice" (formula-driven), which is exactly the profile that rewards a working professional's limited but consistent practice hours more than raw talent or long unbroken study blocks.

cheatSheet: Bayes' theorem: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) / P(B), with P(B) expanded via the law of total probability P(B) = Σ P(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ) — GATE DA's #1 recurring P&S archetype; always draw a probability tree for multi-stage versions.
Independence check: A, B independent ⟺ P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B). Zero correlation does NOT imply independence in general (only under joint normality) — a classic trap.
Variance algebra: Var(aX+b) = a²Var(X); Var(X+Y) = Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y) (drop the covariance term ONLY if X,Y independent/uncorrelated).
Covariance/correlation: Cov(X,Y) = E[XY] − E[X]E[Y]; ρ(X,Y) = Cov(X,Y)/(σ_X σ_Y), always −1 ≤ ρ ≤ 1.
Binomial(n,p): P(X=k) = C(n,k) pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ; mean = np, variance = np(1−p).
Poisson(λ): P(X=k) = e^(−λ) λᵏ/k!; mean = variance = λ. Poisson counts events in an interval — models 'how many'.

Exponential(λ): pdf f(x)=λe^(−λx), mean=1/λ, variance=1/λ². Models waiting time between Poisson events — memoryless: P(X>s+t | X>s)=P(X>t). Poisson vs Exponential is a frequent mix-up: same λ, different question ('how many' vs 'how long until next').
Normal N(μ,σ²): standardize Z=(X−μ)/σ ~ N(0,1); empirical rule ≈68%/95%/99.7% within 1/2/3 σ.
CLT: for large n, sample mean X̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) regardless of the population's original distribution — this is what licenses z/t-based inference on sample means.
Confidence interval for a mean: σ known → X̄ ± z*(σ/√n); σ unknown & n small → X̄ ± t_(n−1)*(s/√n). Choosing z vs t incorrectly is a top scoring error.

Hypothesis testing recipe: state H0/H1 → pick correct test statistic (z, t, or χ²) based on what's known/unknown and sample size → compute test statistic → compare to critical value or use p-value → decide reject/fail-to-reject H0. Chi-squared test degrees of freedom for an r×c contingency table = (r−1)(c−1).
Sample vs population variance: population SD divides by n; sample SD (estimator) divides by (n−1) — a very common NAT-marking-scheme error.

Order of solving on exam: descriptive stats and single-application Bayes/independence items first (cheap, high-accuracy), save multi-step hypothesis-testing/CLT NATs for later given their higher time cost per mark.
commonMistakes: Reversing the direction of conditioning in Bayes'-theorem word problems — computing P(B|A) when the question asks for P(A|B), or misassigning which event is the 'given' vs 'unknown' in a multi-stage tree.
Dropping or mis-signing the covariance/correlation term when computing Var(X+Y) or Var(aX+bY) for dependent random variables.
Using the population standard-deviation formula (divide by n) when the question specifies a sample (should divide by n−1), or vice versa — a frequent silent NAT-marking-scheme killer.

Misidentifying the underlying distribution in a word problem — especially Binomial vs Poisson (finite trials with fixed p vs rate-based counting over a continuous interval) and Poisson vs Exponential (counting events vs waiting time between events).

Picking a z-test where a t-test is required (or vice versa) — forgetting the rule 'population SD known and/or large n → z; population SD unknown and small n → t', and using the wrong degrees of freedom for t/chi-squared tests.
Treating zero correlation as proof of independence — true only under joint normality, false in general; a recurring MSQ trap on 'properties of random variables/distributions'.

Losing marks on MSQ items by treating them like single-answer MCQs (selecting only the most obviously correct option and missing a second correct sub-statement) — costly given MSQs carry no partial credit.

Arithmetic/rounding drift across multi-step NAT problems (chained conditional-probability trees, multi-stage Bayes updates, or hypothesis-testing critical-value lookups) under time pressure, especially without a clear intermediate-value tracking habit.
Forgetting the applicability conditions for the Central Limit Theorem (sample size 'large enough,' i.i.d. assumption) and misapplying a normal approximation to a small/non-i.i.d. sample.
Confusing correlation with causation, or assuming a high |correlation| implies a strong causal or even necessarily linear relationship, when the syllabus only tests the statistical definition.
booksAndResources: Sheldon Ross, 'A First Course in Probability' — the single most cross-source-consistent Probability & Statistics recommendation across GATE DA coaching material (GeeksforGeeks, GO Classes, MathsCare, Applied Course, Analytics Vidhya, ExamPrepTool all name it independently).
Sheldon Ross, 'Introduction to Probability Models' — recommended alongside the above, particularly useful for the random-variables/distributions and expectation chapters.

MIT OCW 6.041/RES.6-012 'Probabilistic Systems Analysis and Applied Probability' (John Tsitsiklis) — the most-cited free video lecture series for this subject across multiple independent GATE DA prep sources; strong for building Bayes'-theorem and distribution intuition from first principles.
GeeksforGeeks 'Probability and Statistics for GATE Exam' notes page — concise formula-first refresher, useful for quick revision given limited study hours.

GATE DA official previous-year question papers (2024 IISc, 2025 IIT Roorkee, 2026 IIT Guwahati) plus GATE Overflow's Probability question bank (gateoverflow.in/questions/mathematics/probability) — highest-value practice source since PYQ style (Bayes word-problems, distribution-ID, hypothesis-testing NATs) has recurred every year so far.

Topic-wise mock/test series covering Probability & Statistics specifically (e.g., GO Classes' DA test series has a dedicated 'Probability and Statistics' topic-wise test) — useful for timed practice on this subject in isolation before attempting full mocks.

Supplementary (well-established engineering-statistics text, not confirmed as a cross-source GATE DA consensus pick but standard for the hypothesis-testing/confidence-interval chapters if Ross's coverage feels thin): Walpole, Myers, Myers & Ye, 'Probability and Statistics for Engineers and Scientists'.

For the ML-overlap payoff of this subject: revisit Naive Bayes (uses Bayes' theorem directly) and LDA (uses covariance/Gaussian assumptions) once P&S fundamentals are solid, to capture the cross-subject marks spillover.
